```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(evtests)
```

Every method in evtests is checked against the numerical results of its
source paper: worked examples are recomputed from the printed data, and
simulation tables are re-run with the published design. This vignette
records, paper by paper, what was reproduced and where a printed value
differs from the value given by the paper's own formulas or design. The
purpose is practical: a user comparing evtests with a published table should
know which differences are expected. The checks themselves are in the
package tests (`tests/testthat/`), where each published value appears next
to the recomputed one.

Throughout, `k` is the number of excesses over the `(k + 1)`-th largest
observation. Some papers count the threshold among the `k` top order
statistics; their `k` is then one more than here.

## Hill (1975)

Table 1 (the 30 largest cities of the United States in 1940, data set
`us_cities_1940`) is reproduced.

* All 29 values of `i V[i]`, `alpha0` and `alpha1` agree to the two printed
  decimals.
* The statistic `H` agrees at two decimals in 24 of 28 rows. For `k` = 15, 26,
  28 and 29 the recomputed values are 13.445, 21.425, 25.825 and 28.239
  (printed 13.45, 21.42, 25.81, 28.23).
* `k C1` agrees to two significant digits in 27 of 29 rows when the
  populations are in inhabitants (the table prints them in thousands). For
  `k = 3` and `k = 28` the recomputed values are 6.24e10 and 7.97e8 (printed
  6.3e10 and 7.9e8).
* The standard deviation ".20 alpha" and the chi-square value ".3" of the
  text are reproduced; the chi-square is .29 with `alpha0` and .32 with
  `alpha1`, and the paper does not say which was used.

```{r}
h <- hill1975(us_cities_1940$population, k = 1:29)
head(h[, c("k", "alpha0", "alpha1", "H")])
```

## Pickands (1975)

The paper has no numerical example. Equation 4.3 prints `exp(-c s)` in the
integral that defines the scale estimate; equations 2.4 and 3.3 have
`exp(c s)`, which is the form implemented. The paper says on p. 122 that the
smallest minimiser should be used to choose `M`, and on p. 130 that the
largest one would be a good choice.

## Grimshaw (1993)

The example of Section 4 (data set `nylon_fibres`) is reproduced: the bounds
`theta_L = -3994.490358` and `h''(0) = -.008455`, the zero `.415834`, the
estimates `k = .117698` and `alpha = .283040`, the log-likelihood 5.697968
and the boundary value 1.985838.

* Several printed values are truncated rather than rounded (the zero is
  .4158348).
* The second zero on `(0, theta_U)` is printed as 1.141551 with
  `(k, alpha, L) = (1.111357, .973553, 2.072396)`. The zero of `h` is at
  1.1415244, with `(k, alpha, L) = (.99963, .87570, 1.985469)`; the printed
  triple corresponds to `theta = 1.1415472`, where `h` is not zero.
* The printed `theta_U = 1.141552` is `1 / max(y)` without the subtraction of
  `eps` described in step 2.
* The note of Table 1 gives a median of .16200; the printed data have median
  .184. The mean, standard deviation and interquartile range of the note
  agree with the data (the interquartile range with quantile type 4).
* The second display of p. 187 has `(1 + k X / alpha)^-1`; the derivation
  and equation 2.2 have `(1 - k X / alpha)^-1`.
* The "approximate 95% upper confidence bound" 9.099524 for the end-point is
  reproduced (9.09945) with the one-sided normal quantile 1.645.

```{r}
fit <- grimshaw1993(nylon_fibres$excess)
fit$zeros
```

## Drees, Ferreira & de Haan (2004)

The paper has no numerical example. The asymptotic variance of Corollary 2.1
is confirmed by simulation. The estimator is defined through a maximum over
`gamma > -1/2`; the paper does not say what to report when the likelihood is
maximised elsewhere.

## Dekkers, Einmahl & de Haan (1989)

The paper has no numerical example.

* In the covariance matrix of equation 3.7, the factor
  `(1 - 3 gamma)(1 - 4 gamma)` of `s22` (for `gamma <= 0`) is printed in the
  numerator; equation 3.10, which follows from it, requires it in the
  denominator. The variance of equation 3.10 is confirmed by simulation.
* The covariance in Lemma 3.4(i) is printed as `2 sqrt(5)`; with unit
  variances it is `2 / sqrt(5)`.
* The sums of exponential spacings in Lemma 4.2 and Theorem 4.3 start at
  `j = i`, which includes `j = 0` in a division by `j`; the Renyi
  representation has `j = i + 1, ..., k`.
* For the end-point estimator, the asymptotic variance of equation 5.3 was
  not confirmed: with generalized Pareto tails (`gamma = -0.5` and `-0.3`,
  `n = 10^7`, `k = 400`, 20000 replicates) the sampling variances were 9.19
  and 88.8, against 8.4 and 70.5 from equation 5.3. `dekkers1989()`
  therefore returns the end-point without an interval.

## Hasofer & Wang (1992)

Hasofer & Wang's `k` counts the threshold, so their `k = 50` is `k = 49`
here.

* The simulations of Tables 1 and 2 (`n = 300`, 50 top order statistics,
  generalized extreme value samples) are reproduced, and so are the powers
  of Table 3 against `gamma > 0`.
* Against `gamma < 0`, the powers of Table 3 are lower than those obtained
  with the critical values of Table 2, by up to .09 (for `gamma = -1/2` at
  level .01, .600 printed against about .69), while the mean and standard
  deviation of `W` agree with Table 1. The paper does not state the critical
  values used for these rows.
* In Table 7, the theoretical mean `1 / 59 = .016949` is printed as .0170.
* Table 8 was interpolated from percentage points of Greenwood's statistic.
  For 30 to 100 order statistics it agrees with the simulated limiting null
  within 1.5% in every column; for 200 the printed points are 1-2% lower;
  for 13 they differ by 2-3%, and the upper 1% point is 2204.6 against about
  2370.

## Neves, Picek & Fraga Alves (2006)

The paper reports powers only in figures, so there is no table to compare
with. The critical values are Gumbel quantiles and are exact. As in Neves &
Fraga Alves (2007), the Hasofer-Wang statistic is printed as
`W = 1 / (k (R - 1))`, while the mean and variance used to standardise it are
those of the original statistic on `k + 1` order statistics. The density of
the loggamma distribution is printed with `Gamma(alpha)` in the denominator
instead of `Gamma(beta)`.

## Neves & Fraga Alves (2007)

Table 1 (generalized Pareto samples, `n = 1000`, 5000 replicates) is
reproduced for both statistics within Monte Carlo error, with one
qualification about the Hasofer-Wang statistic.

* The paper defines `W = 1 / (k (R - 1))` (equations 1.2 and 2.3). With this
  formula the size at `gamma = 0`, `k = 50` is about .072, against .051 in
  the table. The table is reproduced by the original statistic of Hasofer &
  Wang on the `k + 1` largest observations, `W = 1 / ((k + 1) R - k)`, which
  is the one used by `neves_fraga_alves2007()`.
* In Table 1, the power of `R*` at `gamma = -0.4` decreases from .974
  (`k = 150`) to .958 (`k = 200`), while the text states that the power
  increases with `k`.

## Fraga Alves & Neves (2014) and Fraga Alves, Neves & Rosario (2016)

The 2014 paper reports its simulations in figures, and the data of its case
study are not printed. Its Theorem 3 gives an interval for the end-point in
the Gumbel domain, with the scale estimated by the mean excess of the `k`
largest observations, which the paper calls the maximum likelihood estimator
of the generalized Pareto scale (it is that of the exponential distribution).
In simulations of the model of its Section 5 (negative Frechet, `beta = 0.5`,
`n = 1000`, `k = 48`) the nominal 95% interval covered the end-point in all
of 500 samples. For the 2016 paper:

* Table 1 is reproduced for model 4 (Beta tails, `n = 1000`, 300
  replicates): the average absolute errors of the sample maximum and of the
  end-point estimator at the best `k` agree with the printed values (.029
  and .014 for `gamma = -1/2`; .234 and .171 for `gamma = -1/5`).
* The upper bound of equation 14 has no example that can be recomputed (the
  application uses data that are not published with the paper). In our
  simulations of model 4 (1000 to 5000 values, `k` from 25 to 200) the
  coverage of a nominal 95% bound was 0.53-0.68 for `gamma = -0.2` and
  0.85-0.93 for `gamma = -0.4`, in line with the slow convergence the paper
  describes for `gamma` near 0.

## Dietrich, de Haan & Husler (2002) and Husler & Li (2006)

The limiting distributions were simulated (50000 replicates per value of
`gamma`, Brownian motion on 4000 or 20000 points) and reproduce Tables 1 and
2 of Husler & Li (2006) and the row `gamma > 0` of Table 1 of Dietrich et al.

* The last term of the limit of `E` in equation 7 of Dietrich et al. has a
  minus sign; Husler & Li (2006) give it with a plus sign. Simulating with
  the printed sign reproduces the rows `gamma < 0` of Table 1 of Dietrich et
  al.; the corrected sign reproduces Table 1 of Husler & Li, which
  `dietrich2002()` uses.
* In Table 1 of Dietrich et al., the column `p = .95` for `gamma <= -0.5` is
  shifted by one row (printed .635, .635, .750, .886 for `gamma = -0.4` to
  `-0.7`; simulated with the printed sign .637, .764, .928, 1.034).
* In Table 3 of Husler & Li, three cells of the column `p = .70` differ from
  the simulated values: `gamma = .25` (printed .120, simulated about .20),
  `gamma = -.45` (.320 and .27) and `gamma = -.499` (.338 and .28).
* The total relative errors of the `E` test in Table 4 of Husler & Li were not
  reproduced (for example Cauchy .596 simulated against .457 printed); those
  of the `PE` test were.
* Equation 9 of Dietrich et al. prints `B(s) / (s ds)` for the integral of
  `B(s) / s`, and p. 82 refers to a "Pareto with gamma = 0" where `gamma = 1`
  is meant.

## Drees, de Haan & Li (2006)

The PDF available to us is the authors' preprint. Table 1 (limit quantiles
of `k T`) is reproduced by simulation, and the empirical sizes of Tables 6
and 7 are reproduced within Monte Carlo error for most cells.

* The cell `gamma = -0.45`, `p = .995` of Table 1 is printed as 0.739, the
  same value as the cell to its left; the simulated quantile is about 0.81.
* In Table 6 (`n = 200`), the size for the normal distribution at
  `k = 100` is printed as "87", without a decimal point (8.7 is consistent
  with the neighbouring cells).
* For the normal and reversed Burr distributions at large `k` the
  simulated sizes are higher than the printed ones (for example 17.9 against
  12.9), in cells where the maximum likelihood estimate is close to -1/2 and
  depends on the algorithm.

## Wang (1995)

Both examples are printed in full (data sets `bushfires` and
`mice_survival`).

* With the tail allocation not stated in the paper, the examples are
  reproduced with `alpha` shared equally between the two tails: bushfires on
  the log scale, 27 observations; mice at `alpha = 20%`, 8 observations.
* For the bushfires on the original scale at `alpha = 10%` the procedure
  gives 13 observations against 12 printed. The statistic for 13
  observations (0.5956 on Wang's scale) is just inside the acceptance region
  (lower 5% point 0.5816 by simulation, 0.5950 from Table 8 of Hasofer &
  Wang).
* The mice example with an estimated end-point (82 observations) needs an
  end-point estimator taken from other work, and the R-squared criterion
  needs critical values that are not printed; neither is implemented.

## Drees & Kaufmann (1998)

With the recommended constants and `rho = 1`, Tables 1-4 are reproduced
within Monte Carlo error for the Frechet distributions at `n = 500` and
`n = 1000` (for example `gamma = 0.5`, `n = 1000`: RMSE .048). At `n = 100`
the root mean squared error is dominated by a few samples with a very small
selected `k` and varies between simulations. The estimator of `rho` used in
Tables 5-6 is called "modified" without a definition of the modification.

## Guillou & Hall (2001)

* Section 2.2 states the stopping rule as the least `k` with `|T_l| > c`
  for all larger `l`; Section 4.2 as the first `k` in an interval
  `[n^a, n^b]` with `Q_k >= c`. The start of the search is not given.
  `guillou_hall2001()` offers both readings.
* With the first crossing from `k = 2`, the mean selected `k` of Table 1 is
  roughly reproduced for the Frechet and Burr distributions, but the ratios
  `R(c)`, close to 1 in the table, come out between 1.3 and 2.6 under every
  reading we tried.
* The optimal `k` of Table 1 is reproduced for the Burr and Frechet
  distributions but not for the Student distributions (for `t4`, about 8,
  17 and 25 against the printed 4, 9 and 12).
* The expression of `Q(t)` in Section 4.2 integrates `T(u)^2` instead of
  `T(t + u)^2`.

## Danielsson, de Haan, Peng & de Vries (2001)

The formula of Corollary 7 agrees with equations 3.9-3.10 and Corollary 3,
and the mean estimate for the Frechet distribution with `gamma = 0.25` in
Table I is reproduced.

* In Table II, the row Extreme(11) prints a standard error of 0.063 with a
  root mean squared error of 0.004; from the other columns the standard
  error is about 0.003.
* Table III has a row "Extreme(2)", whose numbers are those of Extreme(4).

## Hall & Wang (1999)

The example of Section 3 (data set `olympic_100m`) is reproduced: the
estimate 9.9158 (printed 9.91), the shape 0.826 (printed 0.82; both printed
values truncated), and the interval (9.80, 9.92), which corresponds to a 90%
level; the paper does not state the level. The simulations of Table 1 were
not reproduced: they appear to restrict the search for the end-point to a
range that the paper does not give, and its text says that the values of
`alpha` are less than 2 while the table includes 3, 4 and 5.

## Smith (1985)

The paper has no numerical example.

## Neves & Pereira (2010)

The rejection rates of Figure 1 are reproduced with the standard models
(the statistics are not location invariant).

* Equation 9 gives the limit of `sqrt(k) log(k) T1` as `B1 + B2`; from the
  construction of `T1` it is `B1 - B2`.
* The paper states that `T2*` shifts to the right for distributions in the
  Gumbel domain with a finite end-point; for its own negative Frechet
  example it shifts to the left (mean about -5.5 at `k = 100`), which also
  leads to rejection by the two-sided test.

## Segers & Teugels (2000)

The formulas are confirmed (the score has mean 0 and variance 1/5 under the
null law of Galton's ratio). The paper reports its simulations only in
figures, with which our runs agree as far as they can be read. In the
definition of `Z`, `T(xi_k)` is printed where `T(xi_i)` is meant.

## del Castillo, Daoudi & Lockhart (2014)

* The "Approximate" row of Table 1 is reproduced by the three-moment
  approximation, and the "Asymptotic" row by simulation of Theorem 2.
* The finite-sample 95% points of Table 1 are reproduced within about 0.4
  (0.1 for `n >= 500`); the 99% points of `T_1` to `T_4` differ by up to 1.8
  in both directions, and the printed 99% points are not monotone in `n`.
  The paper does not say how `n / 2^k` is rounded.
* The non-rejection rates under the contaminated null (p. 392, 95.3% to
  98.5%) were not reproduced: a mixture of exponentials has a coefficient of
  variation above 1, and our rates are about 90%.
* The column "HW" of Tables 2 and 3 contains the test of Montfort & Witter
  (MW).

## Choulakian & Stephens (2001)

The Wheaton River example (data set `wheaton_river`, printed to one
decimal) is reproduced approximately, as the rounding of the printed data
allows: deleting the smallest observations one at a time and keeping the
excesses over 27.50, the estimates and statistics of Table 3 agree within
0.015 for the shape, 0.25 for the scale, 0.005 for `W2` and 0.03 for `A2`,
and the procedure stops after six deletions.

* The first row of Table 3 gives `W2 = .2309`; the text gives .2389. The
  recomputed value is .2304.
* In Table 6, the alternative Z(0.25, 0.25) is a mixture of two identical
  generalized Pareto distributions, that is a generalized Pareto
  distribution, for which a power of 94.7% is not possible; the label is
  probably misprinted.
* The text gives the fitted scale for the lognormal as -1.406; Table 7 gives
  1.406.

## Bader, Yan & Zhang (2018)

The p-values of the paper come from a table simulated by the authors that is
not printed; `bader2018()` uses the asymptotic table of Choulakian & Stephens
(2001) instead. The power study and the application are reported in a form
that cannot be recomputed here (figures, and data not printed).
